approachQuestion.prompt:
Terminal Drafts

Two strings first and second contain lowercase English letters and the character #. Reading a string left to right, a letter appends itself to an initially empty draft; # erases the last draft letter if one exists, otherwise it does nothing. Return whether the final drafts are equal. The supplied strings are read-only.

Constraints: each string has length n; 0 <= n <= 200000. Indexed character access is constant time.

Example 1: first = "ab#c", second = "ad#c" -> true (both become "ac").
Example 2: first = "a###", second = "####" -> true (both become empty).
Example 3: first = "a#bc", second = "ab#c" -> false ("bc" versus "ac").
constraints: Choose the most efficient valid approach for the entire stated input domain; accept equivalent optimal variants.

options.text: Walk backward through each string with an independent pending-erasure count. A # adds one; a letter consumes one pending erasure if available, otherwise it is the next survivor. Compare survivors in order and require both streams to exhaust together.
options.feedback: Scanning backward lets each erasure cancel an earlier letter without storing the draft. Independent counts preserve each string's history.

options.text: Build each final draft in a mutable character buffer by appending letters and popping on # when nonempty, then compare the buffers.
options.feedback: This handles every edit correctly, but materializes drafts that can instead be compared as backward survivor streams.

options.text: Remove every # and compare the remaining letters.
options.feedback: For "a#" and "b#", both final drafts are empty, but stripping only # compares a with b.

options.text: Delete every nonoverlapping adjacent letter-# pair from each original string in one pass, remove all remaining # characters, and compare. Do not revisit pairs exposed by deletion.
options.feedback: For "ab##" versus "####", the first becomes "a" by this rule, but both real drafts are empty. An erasure may reach across an earlier canceled pair.

feedback.reason: Traverse an edit history backward with pending erasures, comparing only surviving characters and handling asymmetric exhaustion.
details: Scan backward in each string. Maintain a pending erasure counter while finding the next surviving letter: increase it on #, decrease it on a letter when positive, and otherwise yield the letter. Compare yielded letters. Return true only if all match and both scans finish together.

Backward erasure counting skips characters before yielding survivors. Each hash increases pending deletions; an erased letter consumes one. Compare logical survivors, not raw characters or counts of hashes.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For the fixed method revealed after question 1, choose its tight worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair. Use a word-RAM model with constant-time indexed access and signed 64-bit arithmetic. Include all temporary buffers, input copies, and call frames; exclude supplied input and returned output. n is the length of each supplied string. The fixed method uses index-based iterative scans, no copied strings, draft buffers, recursion, hashing, or amortized operations.
constraints: Analyze this fixed method regardless of your answer to question 1; choose the tightest pair.

options.text: O(n log n) time, O(1) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Backward cursors never revisit characters, even across repeated survivor searches.
details: Each of the two indices only decreases and crosses at most n characters. Even repeated survivor searches do not revisit positions. Some equal inputs require visiting all 2n characters. Two indices, counters, and current characters are fixed storage.

“O(n log n) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: The fixed method does not perform sorting or independent binary searches.
